ledger.hypothesis: This node is ELEMENTWISE, not QUERY -- N=20000 knots and L=20000 links with no inner scan over a second collection, so there is no acceleration structure to build and the win has to come from deleting per-element work and whole-array temporaries. A one-shot instrumented run confirmed it: read=1.80 pre=0.79 solve=0.92 loc=1.86 out=0.47 ms, with only 4 solver iterations -- so the solver was never the bottleneck and `loc` was, and `loc` was almost entirely 20000 Maya 4x4 inverses at ~75 ns each. Only columns 0..2 of each inverse are ever read, so the adjugate gives all of them in ~30 flops. Same reasoning applied to prevM (only row 3 of the product is read) and to phase 1 of the solver (the CSR counting sort fills each knot's bucket in increasing link order, so a link-ordered scatter accumulates into F[i] in exactly the sequence the per-knot gather did -- bit-identical, half the sqrt/divides).
ledger.risk: The adjugate is a different algorithm from Maya's inverse, so the last bits move -- validated at 3.2e-13 worst relative error over 2000 random 4x4 matrices, far inside the 1e-3/1e-4 gate, and nothing here is a comparison that selects a winner, so the tie-break rule does not bite. A det==0 matrix falls back to MMatrix::inverse() so degenerate input behaves exactly as before. The link scatter is the one change that is bit-identical rather than merely within tolerance, because the accumulation ORDER into F[i] is provably unchanged. Nothing was threaded: at 4 iterations the whole solver is 0.65 ms and each pass sits near the ~50 us floor, so a parallel region would have bought little for real race risk.
ledger.theme: Profiled compute() into five sections and removed whole levels of work from the three fattest: replace 20000 general MMatrix::inverse() calls with a direct adjugate that only forms the three columns actually read, build only row 3 of the prev*inverseMatrix product instead of the full 4x4, and walk the spring links once scattering the +/- force to both endpoints instead of recomputing every link twice from each endpoint's adjacency slot.

ledger.hypothesis: profiling said the compute was 40% MArrayDataHandle traversal (1330 us for 6 multis x 20000 elements) and only ONE array input moves between ticks, so invalidating on setDependentsDirty + preEvaluation + an element-count backstop should retire five sixths of that read cost outright; the residual solve time is per-element overhead and whole-array temporaries, not arithmetic, so inlining MMatrix::operator* and deleting positionsPrev/displacements/the per-iteration F fill should take the rest
ledger.risk: the input cache is only as correct as its invalidation -- a dirty route that bypasses BOTH setDependentsDirty and preEvaluation would ship a stale array, which is exactly what parity's re-presented earlier input set is built to catch. The element-count backstop covers a resize but not a same-size value change, so the two dirty hooks are load-bearing. Second risk: the hand-inlined 4x4 product must keep MMatrix's k-order accumulation or curM drifts a ULP; the only comparison it feeds is `det == 0.0`, which is exact either way.
ledger.theme: snapshot every array input in per-instance state and re-walk only the multis that actually went dirty, then inline the matrices*inverseMatrix product and collapse the solver's three redundant 480 KB streams into one fused pass

remeasured.reason: baseline 14.236 ms is below the 15 ms noise floor even at the largest bench scene (geo=400 array=20000); nothing this small can be optimized against measurably
